summary.text: A 76-year-old Caucasian woman with prior myocardial infarction and percutaneous coronary intervention, atrial fibrillation, hyperlipidemia, hypertension and prior ischemic stroke presented to a comprehensive stroke center with chest pain and was found in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response; she was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit and a therapeutic heparin drip was started.

Shortly after admission she developed sudden left hemiparesis, right gaze preference and dysarthria concerning for a right MCA infarction syndrome (NIH stroke score 12, last seen normal ~45 min before detection). The heparin drip was discontinued before CT transport.

Noncontrast head CT showed hyperdensity in the right inferior M2 division; CT angiogram showed an extensively occluded right ICA from its origin, minimal reconstitution of the distal supraclinoid segment, a patent M1 segment and abrupt inferior M2 occlusion.
Because she was within the thrombolysis window, heparin was reversed with protamine sulfate 50 mg IV slow push and, after a 10-minute wait, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg was given by IV push.

Within 20 minutes she improved markedly, with only residual mild left hemiparesis and dysarthria; the neuro-interventional team judged mechanical thrombectomy technically complicated with risks greater than benefit.

Repeat noncontrast CT at ~24 h showed no hemorrhagic transformation or new infarct; MRI around 24 h showed several small acute infarcts in the right MCA distribution (most prominently posterior right insula, also posterior right temporal and right frontal lobes) without hemorrhagic transformation.

She was transitioned to an oral anticoagulant. At outpatient Vascular Neurology follow-up ~1 month later she had no residual symptoms and an NIH Stroke Score of 0. Outpatient carotid duplex showed severe proximal right ICA stenosis, treated with proximal ICA angioplasty and stent placement.
The authors report no hemorrhagic complications, an excellent neurological outcome, and that she continues to do well and is functionally independent.

ambiguities.issue: CT angiography at presentation describes the right ICA as extensively occluded from its origin (Figure 1 caption: absent right ICA), whereas the later outpatient duplex is described as severe proximal right ICA stenosis treated with angioplasty and stenting. The two descriptions come from different modalities at different times, so they are kept as separate supported findings rather than a source_conflict.
ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not reconcile occlusion versus stenosis, infer recanalization, or assume a different vessel segment.

article_limitations: Single case report; the article contains no patient dates, vital signs, laboratory values (including aPTT or heparin dose), or exact clock times, so no time-to-treatment intervals are derived.
Figure pixels are inspected in the separate visual submission; figure annotations here remain caption-level.
Right ICA is described as extensively occluded on CTA at presentation and as severely stenosed on later duplex; the source does not reconcile the two.
Whether mechanical thrombectomy was performed is not explicitly stated; it is recorded only as a team judgement.
Discussion sections cite published studies and guidelines; none of that content is attributed to the index patient.
No supplementary material is listed for this article.
